sections.body_md:
Kawah Ijen closes to **all** visitors — not just JVTO guests — on the first Friday of every month. It has run this way since **March 2019**, for a volunteer conservation program called **"Rijik"** (Javanese for "tidy" / "clean"), during which park staff and volunteers descend into the crater area to remove an estimated **100–150 kg of trash** accumulated from tourism and mining traffic.

It is a small, easily-missed fact — most independent travelers and even some tour operators don't track it — but arriving on a Rijik day means being turned away at the gate after a 01:00 AM wake-up call and a night trek to the crater rim. JVTO checks this calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary, so it never becomes a guest's problem.

sections.title: What Is the Rijik Cleanup Program?
sections.body_md:
Rijik is a scheduled ecosystem-cleaning day at TWA Ijen (the Ijen Nature Tourism Park). On the first Friday of every month, the park closes to tourism and mining traffic so park staff and community volunteers can clear trash from the crater rim, the descent trail, and the shoreline of the sulfur lake — waste that accumulates from the steady flow of tourists and traditional sulfur miners between cleanups.

Each session typically collects an estimated **100–150 kg of trash**. The program has run on this fixed monthly cadence since **March 2019**, making it a predictable, recurring closure rather than an emergency or unplanned event.

sections.title: Why It Matters for Travelers
sections.body_md:
Ijen night hikes are logistically unforgiving: guests are typically picked up from Bondowoso-area hotels around midnight to reach the crater rim in time for the blue-fire window before dawn. If a self-planned or unlicensed itinerary lands on a Rijik closure day, the outcome is a wasted pre-dawn wake-up and a turned-away group at the gate — with no advance warning, because the closure is a park operations detail, not something advertised on ticket-booking pages.

No competitor operator publishes this fact in a dedicated guide. It is exactly the kind of operational detail that separates a licensed operator who tracks park administration from an itinerary assembled purely from generic travel-blog research.

sections.title: How JVTO Handles It
sections.body_md:
- **Checked before confirmation.** JVTO checks the TWA Ijen closure calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary against a guest's requested travel dates.
- **Rerouted, not cancelled.** If a preferred travel window falls on the first Friday of the month, JVTO reorders the itinerary — for example, visiting Bromo or Madakaripura first — so the Rijik closure day never disrupts a confirmed booking. This follows the same alternative-route approach used for PVMBG-driven closures; see [Weather & Closures](/travel-guide/weather-and-closures).
- **Not the same as a safety closure.** Rijik is a fixed conservation closure, unrelated to PVMBG (volcanology) alert-status closures, which are unscheduled and driven by real-time gas and seismic monitoring.
- **Covered by the same cancellation terms.** In the rare case a closure makes a program genuinely unworkable, the standard JVTO Lifetime Package Credit terms apply — see [Booking, Payment & Cancellation Policy](/policy/booking-payment-cancellation).

items.question: Why does Kawah Ijen close on the first Friday of every month?
items.answer: Since March 2019, TWA Ijen (the Ijen Nature Tourism Park) has closed to all visitors on the first Friday of every month for "Rijik" — a scheduled ecosystem-cleaning day. Park staff and volunteers descend into the crater area to remove trash left behind by tourism and mining traffic, typically collecting an estimated 100–150 kg of waste per session. It is a recurring conservation closure, not an emergency shutdown or a sign of a safety incident.

items.question: Will my JVTO tour ever be cancelled because of the Rijik closure day?
items.answer: No. JVTO checks the TWA Ijen closure calendar before confirming any Ijen-inclusive itinerary and schedules guest departures to avoid the first Friday of the month. If a guest's preferred travel window happens to land on a Rijik closure day, JVTO adjusts the itinerary order in advance — for example, visiting Bromo or Madakaripura first — so the closure never disrupts a confirmed booking.

items.question: Is the monthly Ijen closure the same as a PVMBG volcanic-activity closure?
items.answer: No, they are separate and unrelated. Rijik is a fixed, scheduled cleaning day that occurs on the first Friday of every month regardless of volcanic conditions. A PVMBG (Indonesian volcanology agency) closure is unscheduled and happens only when gas emissions or seismic activity cross an official safety threshold. JVTO monitors both: the fixed Rijik calendar for routine scheduling, and real-time PVMBG alerts for safety-driven closures. See Weather & Closures for how PVMBG-driven changes are handled.

items.question: How much trash is removed during the Rijik cleanup at Ijen?
items.answer: Volunteers and park staff typically remove an estimated 100–150 kg of trash from the Kawah Ijen crater area during each monthly Rijik session — waste accumulated from tourism and mining traffic since the previous cleanup.

items.question: When did the Ijen Rijik cleanup program start?
items.answer: The program has run since March 2019, with TWA Ijen closing to visitors on the first Friday of every month for the cleanup. JVTO has scheduled guest itineraries around this fixed closure day for the same period.
